Openly
O-pen-ly
adv.
From open and -ly: publicly, without concealment. Webster 1828: publicly; not in private; without secrecy. Our Lord commands secrecy in giving and promises an open reward, and Paul uses the word for the public humiliation of the powers at the cross.

Biblical Definition

The Sermon on the Mount sets secrecy and openness in a deliberate order: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly (Matthew 6:4). The concealment is the disciple’s work; the publication is God’s, and it is promised. Christ Himself moved differently at different times, and John records a moment of deliberate reserve: when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret (John 7:10) — His hour was not yet come, and He would not be managed by relatives urging a public display. Paul uses the word for what the cross did to the hostile powers: having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it (Colossians 2:15) — the imagery is a Roman triumph, the conquered paraded in public. And Peter is careful about the limits of the resurrection appearances: Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly; not to all the people, but unto witnesses chosen before of God (Acts 10:40-41).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OPENLY as publicly; not in private; without secrecy; and also plainly, evidently, without disguise or reserve.

OPENLY, adv. — Publicly; not in private; without secrecy.

Plainly; evidently; without disguise or reserve.

OPEN, a. — Unclosed; not shut; free of access; public; not concealed.

OPEN, v.t. — To unclose; to set open; to make plain; to reveal or disclose.

Anglo-Saxon open; the adverbial -ly from lic, like.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:4 — "That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly."

John 7:10 — "But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret."

Colossians 2:15 — "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."

Acts 10:40 — "Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly;"

Modern Corruption

Matthew 6 makes concealment the disciple’s duty and publication God’s prerogative, which is the direct opposite of a religious culture built on documented and shared good works.

expand to see more

Our Lord’s instruction is not that giving should be modest but that it should be hidden — the left hand not knowing what the right does — and the reason He gives is blunt: those who give to be seen of men have their reward, receiving in full and at once the only payment they were after. The modern practice of documenting and circulating one’s charitable acts, whether by a ministry publishing its numbers or an individual posting them, cannot be reconciled with the paragraph merely by pleading good motives, because the passage addresses the practice and not only the heart behind it. Where the giving must be known for administrative reasons, Scripture provides for that too (2 Corinthians 8:20-21); what it forbids is the giving whose visibility is the point.

Colossians 2:15 gives the word its most triumphant use, and the picture is worth recovering because it inverts every appearance at Calvary. To every eye present, the powers had made a public spectacle of Christ; Paul says Christ made the public spectacle of them, spoiling principalities and powers and leading them in triumph. This is the answer to the persistent instinct that the cross was a defeat God afterwards reversed. The Reformed doctrine of the atonement holds the cross itself as the victory — sin borne, wrath satisfied, the accuser disarmed — with the resurrection as its public vindication. Acts 10:40 adds the sober qualification about that vindication: God shewed Him openly, but to chosen witnesses, not indiscriminately, which is why the church rests on apostolic testimony rather than on general spectacle.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek en to phanero, in the open, openly; parresia (G3954), boldness, openness of speech; deigmatizo (G1165), to make a public example of; emphanes (G1717), manifest.

expand to see more

Greek en to phanero — in the open; the promised reward of Matthew 6:4.

Greek parresia (G3954) — freedom of speech, openness; not openly in John 7:10 is literally not in parresia.

Greek deigmatizo (G1165) — to make a public example or spectacle of; made a shew of them openly (Colossians 2:15).

Greek thriambeuo (G2358) — to lead in triumph, as a Roman general; the verb of the same verse.

Greek emphanes (G1717) — manifest, visible; shewed him openly (Acts 10:40).

Usage

"Thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly (Matthew 6:4) — concealment is the disciple’s work, publication is God’s."

"Not openly, but as it were in secret (John 7:10) — Christ refusing to be managed into a public display."

"He made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it (Colossians 2:15) — the spectacle at Calvary inverted."
